newsitem.title: GERMANY: Lauda Air sees Germany flights cut under AUA deal.
newsitem.headline: Lauda Air sees Germany flights cut under AUA deal.

text.p: Lauda Air said it might have to drop flights to Germany under its planned strategic cooperation with Austrian Airlines (AUA).

Services from Vienna to Frankfurt, Duesseldorf and Munich could be reduced or dropped entirely from this winter to cut competition to AUA on the same routes, the airline's general manager Germany, Michael Svedek, told Reuters in an interview.
"The changes will be greatest in Germany. We are certainly the smallest of the four airlines flying between Germany and Austria," he said.
Austrian, following its purchase of a 36 percent stake in Lauda Air, has said it will remain the main scheduled carrier and Lauda will serve leisure destinations.

Lauda currently flies from Vienna daily to Frankfurt and twice-daily to Duesseldorf and Munich as well as from Salzburg four times daily to Frankfurt and daily to Berlin with all flights as code-shares with Deutsche Lufthansa AG.
AUA and Lufthansa both have more flights than Lauda on the same routes from Vienna.
Svedek said: "It could be that we give up Frankfurt and Duesseldorf, or AUA puts in a larger aircraft or we get other routes.
"With Duesseldorf and Munich, if AUA flies there, then perhaps it would be better for Lauda not to fly," he added.
But he stressed: "Even if we go off-line, then we will still be present as a code-share flight and will have better connecting flights to long-haul services."
Svedek added: "We have built up these Germany routes successfully and of course it would hurt us to lose them. It would be a shame for everything to happen quickly."
It was an open question whether the existing code-sharing between Lauda and Lufthansa would become a three-way code-share with AUA on Germany-Austria flights, Svedek said.
It was unlikely all the changes would go into effect from winter 1997-98, he added.
Co-ordinated flights and sales cooperation could boost AUA's Germany traffic and generate more passengers for Lauda's long-haul leisure flights from Vienna, Svedek pointed out.
There were no plans to close Lauda's German offices and integrate staff into the joint sales operations of AUA, Swissair and Sabena, he added.
Lauda had no real long-haul route conflicts with AUA since Lauda already concentrated on tourist destinations such as Australia, south-east Asia and Florida, he noted.
